administration.subject: Social Studies
administration.teksAlignmentVintage: Post-streamlining Grade 8 Social Studies TEKS. Every SE code used on this form is still listed in TEA's current assessed curriculum.
administration.note: This is the last Grade 8 Social Studies administration for which TEA published a full PDF test form. From 2023 onward STAAR is administered primarily online and TEA states that 'PDF versions of STAAR released tests are no longer available'.

capture.scope: Items whose TEA-published content student expectation is one of the 23 Boston chapter SEs, plus item 22 (8.16(A), not a Boston SE) because the repo already carries a paraphrase of it.
capture.method: Item text transcribed from TEA's released form PDF text layer. Correct answers taken from TEA's official student-expectations-tested table, never inferred from the item.

stimulus.title: U.S. Enslaved Population by Select Region, 1840

items.stem: Which statement describes a factor that MOST contributed to the population difference shown in the table?

options.text: The South had a society that relied on wage labor.
The South had an economy that relied on cotton.
The South had a variety of natural resources.
The South had an abundance of large cities.

items.usabilityNote: Correct SE, wrong era and region for Boston.

items.bostonConcept: Boston Act 4 gated fact: Intolerable / Coercive Acts
items.stem: How did the American colonies react to enforcement of the Intolerable Acts?

options.text: By collecting funds to pay for the tea destroyed in Boston Harbor
By sending ambassadors to France to request military aid
By placing a tax on all goods imported from Great Britain
By holding the First Continental Congress to discuss unified resistance

repoLinkage.relationship: The repo item is a condensed paraphrase of this released item and carries the same key (J). The repo's tag 8.4(A):INTOLERABLE_ACTS agrees with TEA's published label.

items.captureReason: Not one of the 23 Boston SEs. Captured only because the repo carries a paraphrase of it (BANK.BOSTON.USER.Q22.v1) and the retagging pass needs its true provenance. Content is quartering, which Boston does dramatize, but TEA assessed it as an amendment-purpose item.
items.stem: Why was the Third Amendment prohibiting the quartering of troops added to the U.S. Constitution?

options.text: To address colonial treatment by the British military
To maintain control over members of the British military
To ensure the national government could pay for the U.S. military
To reinforce the need for state militias in the United States

repoLinkage.relationship: The repo item is a condensed paraphrase of this released item and carries the same key (F). The repo tags it TEKS.PENDING_SME_REVIEW; TEA's published label is 8.16(A), which is NOT one of Boston's 23 SEs.

items.bostonRelevance: 8.20(A) civic virtue is a Boston pattern carried by Samuel Adams and John Adams as NPC exemplars. This item uses Jefferson.
items.stem: Why is Thomas Jefferson’s writing of the Declaration of Independence considered to be one of his greatest contributions to American history?

options.text: He showed responsibility by outlining the structure for a new government.
He helped define rights that would defeat tyranny.
He developed a military plan to defeat the British.
He outlined a strategy for acquiring the Louisiana Territory.

repoLinkage.relationship: The repo item is a condensed paraphrase of this released item and carries the same key (B). The repo tags it TEKS.PENDING_SME_REVIEW; TEA's published label is 8.20(A).

items.bostonRelevance: Quotes Samuel Adams, a Boston 8.4(B) individual, in 1772, inside the chapter's Act 3 window. Carries both Boston's 8.3(A) representative-government pattern and its 8.19(A) natural-rights pattern in one stimulus. The single most Boston-native released item outside 8.4(A).

stimulus.text: Among the natural rights of the Colonists are these: First, a right to life; Secondly, to liberty; Thirdly, to property; together with the right to support and defend them in the best manner they can.

items.stem: In the early days of the colonies, a belief in these rights helped lead to —

options.text: the implementation of the mercantile system

repoLinkage.relationship: The repo item is a condensed paraphrase of this released item and carries the same key (G). The repo tags it 8.4(A):NO_REPRESENTATION; TEA's published label is 8.3(A). This is a real mis-tag in the repo, not a vintage difference.

stimulus.title: American Platform of Principles, 1857
stimulus.note: Presented as a period political slogan graphic. The slogan text is captured verbatim; the graphic treatment is not.

items.stem: What motivated some people to support this nativist slogan?

options.text: An affirmation of states’ rights by Jefferson Davis and the belief that tariffs are un-American
Large-scale immigration to cities and the belief that immigrants stole jobs from native-born citizens
The desire for an independent country free from foreign rule and unfair mercantile economic policies
A rejection of anti-American influence following the Battle of San Jacinto and the addition of new territories

items.usabilityNote: Correct SE, wrong era for Boston. Both released 8.23(B) items are 19th-century nativism; neither touches the urban conflict Boston uses this SE for.

stimulus.text: Agriculture, manufactures, commerce, and navigation, the four pillars of our prosperity, are the most thriving when left most free to individual enterprise.
stimulus.attribution: —President Thomas Jefferson, first annual message, December 8, 1801

items.stem: Which economic principle is President Jefferson showing support for in this excerpt?
items.usabilityNote: 8.14(A) explicitly names 'minimal government regulation, taxation, and property rights', and this item tests the regulation branch. Boston uses 8.14(A) via the economy and trade systems in mission M4.

items.stem: Which human geographic factor helped the Union win the Civil War?

options.text: A network of railroads in the North allowed Union soldiers to be moved quickly over long distances.
The Oregon Trail allowed Union military supplies to be moved quickly to the West.
Northern farms started producing cotton used to make Union military uniforms.
Canals in the Midwest allowed food for Union soldiers to be moved quickly to the front lines.

items.usabilityNote: Correct SE, wrong era. The transportation-network reasoning is the same shape Boston needs for the rider run and committees of correspondence.
